message.content: {"passages":[{"reference":"5.11","text":"But let every door be opened to him, and let all wicked and imposed laws laid down for jealous people be annulled. Such people, controlled by folly and unwilling to understand what is reasonable, while also looking suspiciously upon those called adulterers, are appropriately made sport of by Zeus himself, through Minos and Rhadamanthus, with enacted laws. For when Eros has come to dwell in souls, it is impossible to restrain him, since the passion of lovers is not voluntary. Indeed, Zeus himself, the lawgiver of these laws, had intercourse with countless women. Some wise men praise him as a benefactor toward procreation, because he grants human beings intercourse with himself; but among those by whom he knew himself to be unrecognized with respect to the favor, he transformed his appearance, so that he might neither distress them nor appear to act against the laws established by himself. Therefore, one who devotes herself to philosophy for the sake of a noble life must imitate those acknowledged to be superior, whose couplings have been countless.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"πάντες δὲ μοχθηροὶ καὶ θετοὶ λυέσθωσαν νόμοι","chosen":"let all wicked and imposed laws ... be annulled","rationale":"θετός denotes a law laid down or enacted, in contrast to what is natural; “imposed” retains that force."},{"source_quote":"ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ τοῦ Διὸς διά γε τοῦ Μίνωος καὶ τοῦ Ῥαδαμάνθυος εὐλόγως θετοῖς παίζονται νόμοις","chosen":"are appropriately made sport of by Zeus himself, through Minos and Rhadamanthus, with enacted laws","rationale":"Zeus is the agent, Minos and Rhadamanthus are intermediaries, and the dative νόμοις supplies the means; εὐλόγως may qualify either the mockery or the enactment."},{"source_quote":"Ἔρωτα γὰρ ἐπιδημήσαντα ψυχαῖς","chosen":"when Eros has come to dwell in souls","rationale":"The personal name and participle preserve the image of Eros arriving and taking up residence rather than reducing it to an abstract feeling."},{"source_quote":"παρ’ οἷς δὲ ἐπὶ τῷ χάριτι ἠπίστατο ἀγνοούμενος","chosen":"but among those by whom he knew himself to be unrecognized with respect to the favor","rationale":"The construction is compressed. χάριτι may denote his favor, especially the sexual favor just mentioned, while ἀγνοούμενος says that he was unrecognized; “not favorably recognized” or “not welcomed for the favor” are also possible."},{"source_quote":"τῇ φιλοσοφίᾳ προσανέχουσαν","chosen":"one who devotes herself to philosophy","rationale":"The participle is feminine singular; the English explicitly preserves the otherwise implicit female referent."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"5.12","text":"And so that I may not waste time in vain on the more numerous demonstrations, I shall begin with Zeus himself, the father of gods and human beings, and disclose some of his unions, for it is impossible to recall them all because of their multitude. Listen, then, to the unions of great Zeus himself that remained hidden through transformation because of the jealousy of foolish men. For first, wishing to resolve for the wise the suspected sin of adultery in varied intercourse, when he was about to marry, he knew that although most people would regard him as an adulterer at the first bedding, he was not becoming one; and through the apparent sin, as I said, he procured a sinless marriage. For he marries Hera, who is his sister, after being made like a cuckoo in plumage, and from her Hebe and Eileithyia came into being. For he gives birth to Metis without intercourse with anyone, just as Hera also gives birth to Hephaestus.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"τὰς ἐνίων μηνύειν κοινωνίας","chosen":"disclose some of his unions","rationale":"ἐνίων is taken partitively in light of the following contrast with all of the unions."},{"source_quote":"τὰς διὰ τῆς μεταμορφώσεως λανθανούσας κοινωνίας","chosen":"the unions ... that remained hidden through transformation","rationale":"λανθάνω emphasizes escaping notice, while μεταμόρφωσις supplies the means of concealment."},{"source_quote":"τῆς διαφόρου μίξεως","chosen":"in varied intercourse","rationale":"διάφορος can mean diverse or different; “intercourse with another” is a possible alternative, but the surrounding catalogue favors repeated intercourse in differing forms."},{"source_quote":"ὡς ἐπὶ πρώτῃ εὐνῇ κατὰ τοὺς πολλοὺς μοιχὸς εἰδὼς οὐ γινόμενος","chosen":"he knew that although most people would regard him as an adulterer at the first bedding, he was not becoming one","rationale":"The negation is retained with γινόμενος. κατὰ τοὺς πολλούς is understood as marking popular judgment rather than the narrator’s own conclusion."},{"source_quote":"ὁμοιωθεὶς κόκκυγος πτερῷ","chosen":"after being made like a cuckoo in plumage","rationale":"Literally the comparison is to a cuckoo’s wing or feather; “in plumage” expresses the respect in which the likeness is asserted without replacing the cuckoo image."},{"source_quote":"τὴν Μῆτιν ... ἀποκυΐσκει","chosen":"he gives birth to Metis","rationale":"ἀποκυΐσκω denotes bringing forth or giving birth, and the supplied object is explicitly Metis."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"τὴν Μῆτιν γὰρ χωρὶς τῆς πρὸς τινὰ μίξεως ἀποκυΐσκει","issue":"The printed wording clearly names Metis as the one Zeus brings forth. This is mythographically unexpected, since a familiar account instead has Zeus bring forth Athena after swallowing Metis, but the supplied reading is intelligible and has therefore been translated without harmonization.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"5.13","text":"Furthermore, he has intercourse with a sister of his who came into being from Uranus and Thalassa as a result of the cutting performed by Cronus, . . . . Eros and Cypris, whom they also call Didone. He also has intercourse with Antiope daughter of Nycteus, taking the likeness of a satyr, and from her Amphion and Zethus came into being. He has relations with Alcmene, the wife of Amphitryon, after being made like Amphitryon, the man who had married her, and from her Heracles came into being. He approaches Aegina daughter of Asopus after becoming an eagle, and from her Aeacus is born. He lies with Amalthea daughter of Phocus after being made like a bear. He flowed over Danae daughter of Acrisius as gold, and from her Perseus flew up. For Callisto daughter of Lycaon he became a fierce lion, and she bears another Arcas. He had intercourse with Europa daughter of Phoenix by means of a bull, and from her Minos, Rhadamanthus, and Sarpedon sprang forth. For Eurymedusa daughter of Achelous he became an ant, and from her came Myrmidon. For the nymph of Hersaeus he became a vulture, and from her came the Palici in Sicily. He had intercourse with Himalia the earthborn on Rhodes by means of rain, and from her came Spartaeus, Cronius, and Cytus. He took Cassiepeia as a bride after being made like Phoenix, the man who had married her, and from her Atymnius sprang forth for him. For Nemesis daughter of Thestius, who was also thought to be Leda, he became a swan or a goose and fathered Helen; and again, after becoming a star, he brought Castor and Polydeuces to light. For Lamia he assumed the form of a hoopoe.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ἀπὸ τῆς Κρόνου ἐκτομῆς","chosen":"as a result of the cutting performed by Cronus","rationale":"The wording denotes Cronus’s act of cutting; this avoids the misleading implication that Cronus himself was castrated."},{"source_quote":"ἣν καὶ Διδώνην λέγουσιν","chosen":"whom they also call Didone","rationale":"The translation preserves the printed name Διδώνην rather than silently replacing it with the mythologically familiar Dione."},{"source_quote":"Καλλιστοῖ τῇ Λυκάονος ἠγριώθη λέων","chosen":"For Callisto daughter of Lycaon he became a fierce lion","rationale":"ἠγριώθη conveys becoming wild or fierce, while λέων supplies the lion image."},{"source_quote":"Ἑρσαίου νύμφῃ","chosen":"for the nymph of Hersaeus","rationale":"The genitive is rendered directly. The precise identity intended by the unfamiliar name is uncertain, so it is not replaced with a figure from another mythographic form."},{"source_quote":"Κασσιέπειαν ἐνύμφευσεν","chosen":"He took Cassiepeia as a bride","rationale":"The active verb can denote making someone a bride or giving her in marriage; the catalogue of Zeus’s unions and the following disguise support the contextual rendering “took ... as a bride.”"},{"source_quote":"ἀστὴρ γενόμενος ... ἐξέφηνεν","chosen":"after becoming a star, he brought ... to light","rationale":"The rendering preserves both the stellar transformation and the manifestation imagery of ἐκφαίνω."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"ἀπὸ τῆς Κρόνου ἐκτομῆς, . . . . Ἔρως καὶ Κύπρις","issue":"The selected edition prints a lacuna of exactly four dots between the surviving clauses. Its content is unavailable; the English retains all four dots, and no restoration has been supplied. The wording after the gap consequently remains syntactically fragmentary.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false},{"source_quote":"Διδώνην","issue":"The printed proper name is Didone, although Dione would be expected as an epithet or identification of Cypris in familiar mythographic wording. The printed form is retained in the translation.","proposed_reading":"Διώνην (conjectural; not adopted)","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"5.14","text":"He himself assumes a shepherd’s likeness and makes Mnemosyne the mother of the Muses. He marries Semele daughter of Cadmus while blazing, and from her brings Dionysus to completion. He himself takes his own daughter Persephone as a bride, after being made like a serpent—she who was also believed to be the wife of his brother Pluto. He also has intercourse with many others even without transformation, since the husbands feel no jealousy as though over a sin, but know well that, by freely having intercourse with their wives, he begets children and bestows upon them Hermeses, Apollos, Dionysuses, Endymions, and however many others we have mentioned, all exceptionally distinguished in beauty as a result of intercourse with him.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"Μνημοσύνην ... Μουσῶν ἀποφαίνει μητέρα","chosen":"makes Mnemosyne the mother of the Muses","rationale":"ἀποφαίνω can mean show, declare, or cause to appear; in this catalogue of unions, “makes ... the mother” conveys the resulting maternity."},{"source_quote":"πυρσέων","chosen":"while blazing","rationale":"The unusual form is understood from its transparent association with πυρσός, “firebrand” or “blaze,” without silently replacing the printed word."},{"source_quote":"ἐξ ἧς Διόνυσον τελεῖ","chosen":"from her brings Dionysus to completion","rationale":"τελέω means complete or bring to fulfillment; the wording may allude to Dionysus’s completed gestation rather than merely using a generic verb for begetting."},{"source_quote":"Περσεφόνην αὐτὸς ἐκνυμφεύει τὴν θυγατέρα","chosen":"He himself takes his own daughter Persephone as a bride","rationale":"Although the active verb can mean give in marriage, the serpent transformation and surrounding list of Zeus’s unions support the reflexive contextual sense “takes ... as a bride.”"},{"source_quote":"χαριζόμενος αὐτοῖς Ἑρμεῖς, Ἀπόλλωνας, Διονύσους, Ἐνδυμίωνας","chosen":"bestows upon them Hermeses, Apollos, Dionysuses, Endymions","rationale":"The source deliberately uses plural forms of the names, presenting such beautiful offspring as repeated types; the plurals are preserved."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"Σεμέλην τὴν Κάδμου πυρσέων γαμεῖ","issue":"The printed form πυρσέων is morphologically unusual in this construction. It may be an uncontracted participial form associated with πυρσός, supporting the fire imagery used in the translation; alternatively, the text may reflect a defective writing of πυρσὸς ὤν, “being a firebrand.”","proposed_reading":"Σεμέλην τὴν Κάδμου πυρσὸς ὢν γαμεῖ (conjectural; not adopted)","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"5.15","text":"And so that I may not spend time on an endless exposition, you will find that all the gods, together with Zeus, have unstinting unions, which fools call adulteries of the gods. Even the male gods do not avoid such couplings as shameful, but practice this too as something seemly. Indeed, Zeus himself loves Ganymede; Poseidon loves Pelops; Apollo loves Cinyras, Zacynthus, Hyacinthus, Phorbas, Hylas, Admetus, Cyparissus, Amyclas, Troilus, Branchus, Atymnius, Paros, Potnieus, and Orpheus—Dionysus loves Adonis, Ampelus, Hymenaeus, Hermaphroditus, and Achilles—Asclepius loves Hippolytus—and Hephaestus loves Peleus—Pan loves Daphnis—Hermes loves Perseus, Chrysus, Thersus, and Odrysus—and Heracles loves Abderus, Dryops, Iocastus, Philoctetes, Ilas, Polyphemus, Haemon, Diomus, and Pirithous.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"πάντων μετὰ Διὸς θεῶν ἀφθόνους ... κοινωνίας","chosen":"all the gods, together with Zeus, have unstinting unions","rationale":"μετά with the genitive means “with,” and ἄφθονος conveys abundance or lack of restraint."},{"source_quote":"μηδὲ τῶν ἀρρένων τὰς μίξεις φυλασσομένων ὡς αἰσχράς","chosen":"Even the male gods do not avoid such couplings as shameful","rationale":"τῶν ἀρρένων is taken as the subject of the genitive participle. It can alternatively be attached to μίξεις as “couplings with males”; the following all-male catalogue makes the same-sex reference clear in either construction."},{"source_quote":"ἀλλὰ ἐπιτηδευόντων καὶ τοῦτο ὡς εὐπρεπές","chosen":"but practice this too as something seemly","rationale":"ἐπιτηδεύω denotes deliberately practicing or pursuing something, while εὐπρεπές contrasts what is seemly with what is shameful."},{"source_quote":"Ἴλα","chosen":"Ilas","rationale":"The transliteration preserves the printed smooth-breathing form and distinguishes it from Ὕλα, rendered “Hylas,” earlier in the same list."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"Ἴλα","issue":"The printed form denotes Ilas and differs from the earlier Ὕλα, Hylas. Since Heracles is commonly associated with Hylas, the form may be a proper-name variant or a copying or printing error, but the selected reading is clear and has not been normalized.","proposed_reading":"Ὕλα (conjectural; not adopted)","blocks_publication":false}]}]}
